Place two queens on a chessboard and say whether they can attack each other.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/queen-attack) (MIT). Listed under [Games & Simulation](/examples/?subject=games-and-simulation).

```nomi-run
// FILE: queen_attack.nomi
//# Whether two queens on a chessboard can attack each other.

/// A queen on an 8 by 8 board, at a zero-based row and column.
pub opaque struct Queen {
    row: Int
    column: Int
}

impl Queen {
    /// Places a queen, or says which coordinate is off the board.
    pub fn new(row: Int, column: Int) -> Result<Queen, Error> {
        case {
            row < 0 -> Err(.RowNotPositive)
            row > 7 -> Err(.RowNotOnBoard)
            column < 0 -> Err(.ColumnNotPositive)
            column > 7 -> Err(.ColumnNotOnBoard)
            _ -> Ok(#Queen{row, column})
        }
    }

    /// Reports whether two queens share a row, a column or a diagonal.
    pub fn can_attack(white: Queen, black: Queen) -> Bool {
        rows = Int.abs(white.row - black.row)
        columns = Int.abs(white.column - black.column)
        rows == 0 or columns == 0 or rows == columns
    }
}

/// Why a queen cannot be placed.
pub enum Error {
    RowNotPositive
    RowNotOnBoard
    ColumnNotPositive
    ColumnNotOnBoard
}

// FILE: queen_attack_test.nomi
import queen_attack.{Error, Queen}

group "Test creation of Queens with valid and invalid positions" {
    test "queen with a valid position" {
        assert Queen.new(2, 2)
    }

    test "invalid positions" {
        cases = [
            #("queen must have positive row", -2, 2, Error.RowNotPositive),
            #("queen must have row on board", 8, 4, .RowNotOnBoard),
            #("queen must have positive column", 2, -2, .ColumnNotPositive),
            #("queen must have column on board", 4, 8, .ColumnNotOnBoard),
        ]

        subtests cases, #(description, row, column, error), description {
            assert Queen.new(row, column) == Err(error)
        }
    }
}

test "Test the ability of one queen to attack another" {
    cases = [
        #("cannot attack", #(2, 4), #(6, 6), False),
        #("can attack on same row", #(2, 4), #(2, 6), True),
        #("can attack on same column", #(4, 5), #(2, 5), True),
        #("can attack on first diagonal", #(2, 2), #(0, 4), True),
        #("can attack on second diagonal", #(2, 2), #(3, 1), True),
        #("can attack on third diagonal", #(2, 2), #(1, 1), True),
        #("can attack on fourth diagonal", #(1, 7), #(0, 6), True),
        #(
            "cannot attack if falling diagonals are only the same when reflected across the longest falling diagonal",
            #(4, 1),
            #(2, 5),
            False,
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(
        description,
        #(white_row, white_column),
        #(black_row, black_column),
        expected
    ), description {
        assert Ok(white) = Queen.new(white_row, white_column)
        assert Ok(black) = Queen.new(black_row, black_column)
        assert Queen.can_attack(white, black) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- `Queen` is a `pub opaque struct`, so `Queen.new` is the only way to build one and an off-board queen cannot exist.
- `Queen.new` validates with a subject-less `case`, one arm per canonical error, and answers `Result<Queen, Error>`.
- `can_attack` compares row and column distances, each `Int.abs` of a difference: equal rows, equal columns or equal distances.
- The valid-position case is its own test (`assert Queen.new(2, 2)`), since an opaque `Queen` cannot be written as an expected value outside its file.
- The attack table builds each queen with `assert Ok(white) = Queen.new(...)`; `?` cannot be used in a `subtests` body, and the error saying so suggests this form.
